identity_rationale: Theodor W. Adorno, identified by Philosophical Fragments (limited circulation, with Max Horkheimer) and Dialectic of Enlightenment (revised publication, with Max Horkheimer). Existing curated person ID reused; no new authority ID or namesake merger.

screening.role: Selection context only, not substantive proof or automatic identity resolution.

sources.note: New limited rereading: opening from the sociological theory of cultural chaos through standardization, economic power and technology; later selected paragraphs from Amusement and all the elements through the high/light-art division and amusement as a prolongation of work. Intervening and later body unread. Joint Horkheimer/Adorno authorship and host’s missing precise English-edition/translator retained; generalizations remain attributed arguments.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Theodor W. Adorno: selected publication history and bibliography
sources.note: Only biography/work paragraphs, section 3 opening and selected bibliography entries checked: limited Philosophical Fragments circulation 1944; revised Dialectic of Enlightenment 1947, both with Horkheimer; Minima Moralia 1951; Negative Dialectics 1966. These publication facts do not establish complete reading; no detailed argument is inferred from the bibliography.

sources.title: Goethe University Frankfurt, Archive of the Institute for Social Research collection description
sources.note: Institutional archival description explicitly identifies Theodor W. Adorno (1903–1969), distinct from Max Horkheimer (1895–1973). Collection description only, not underlying personal papers; year-only life precision.

substantive_relations.relationship: With Horkheimer, connects standardized cultural production to economic power rather than autonomous technological necessity.
substantive_relations.note: Joint primary chapter opening read. Authorship is collective; this does not attribute the whole chapter solely to Adorno or adopt its sweeping cultural judgments as findings.

substantive_relations.relationship: With Horkheimer, analyzes amusement’s continuity with work and the historical split between light and serious art.
substantive_relations.note: Joint primary chapter selected later paragraphs read. A conceptual resource for analyzing mass culture, not proof of direct transmission to all British cultural studies or a claim that popular art has no value.

limits: Selected theoretical contributions and dated texts, with original, revised, translated and posthumous forms distinguished. Source notes state actual reading extent; no complete monograph or comprehensive reception survey is claimed. Existing collective relationships and source/roster qualifications remain.
